title: Launchpad
teaches: The launchpad as we trade it: after a real correction a stock rests five weeks or more under three averages pinched within 3% of price near a flat 200-day, the launch bar closes above all four averages up 2% or more in the top of its range, the stop sits a few cents under the launch day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the 20 EMA trail, and the stock, the base and the market, not the bar, carry the edge.

facts.quote: The Launch Pad Setup occurs when price reclaims important KMAs to the upside on volume.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the Launch Pad is price reclaiming its key moving averages on volume.

facts.quote: Price trades underneath the KMAs in a base
facts.claim: TraderLion step one: price trades underneath the key averages in a base.

facts.quote: Price reclaims these KMAs to the upside
facts.claim: TraderLion step two: price reclaims the averages.

facts.quote: The KMAs start to curl underneath price, forming a Launch Pad for higher prices
facts.claim: TraderLion step three: the averages curl underneath price, forming the launch pad.

facts.quote: Price retests the KMAs & bounces off of them
facts.claim: TraderLion step four: price retests the averages and bounces.

facts.quote: the Power of 3 Setup occurs when a stock goes from trading below its 10, 21, and 50-day Simple Moving Averages to trading above in a single session.
facts.claim: Rai: the Power of 3 is a stock going from below its 10, 21 and 50-day averages to above them in one session.

facts.quote: Moving averages should be horizontal as price breaks through. Downtrending MAs decrease the probability of success of the setup.
facts.claim: Rai: the averages should be horizontal as price breaks through; falling averages hurt the odds.

facts.quote: Stop techniques usually all revolve around the stock breaking below recent lows (preferably within 3-5% of entry price) or multi-day closes below the moving averages of interest.
facts.claim: Rai: stops sit under recent lows, preferably within 3 to 5% of the entry.

facts.quote: a stock's key moving averages converge to the upside in a tight bunch beneath price.
facts.claim: Haber: the key averages converge in a tight bunch beneath price.

facts.quote: Tight relative to itself. The bunch should be visibly tighter than the averages were during the prior decline or base.
facts.claim: Haber: tight means visibly tighter than the averages were during the prior decline.

facts.quote: A pile of flat averages above price is a ceiling, not a launchpad.
facts.claim: Haber: flat averages above price are a ceiling, not a launchpad.

facts.quote: A launchpad forming on an early-stage base at the start of a new uptrend carries far more weight than one forming after the stock has already doubled.
facts.claim: Haber: an early-stage launchpad carries far more weight than one after the stock has doubled.

facts.quote: Wide, loose stocks with huge average daily ranges can form something that looks like a launchpad, but it's often a trap
facts.claim: Haber: wide, loose stocks with huge daily ranges form launchpad look-alikes that are often a trap.

facts.quote: If the distance is more than 3%, the entry isn't there yet. Wait, or pass.
facts.claim: Haber: if the stop is more than 3% away, wait or pass.

facts.quote: In each bull market cycle, the strongest stocks will pause their advance, consolidate their recent gains, form a new base, and then break out to even higher levels.
facts.claim: Deepvue: the strongest stocks pause, consolidate, form a new base, then break out.

facts.quote: A protective stop can then be placed at the opposite end of the range.
facts.claim: Deepvue puts the stop at the other end of the tight range.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: a climax run on your own long: sell a big part into it.

facts.quote: Prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings; the chart comes first.
facts.claim: D40: growing sales and earnings preferred; the chart comes first.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: Close of $10 or more and $20 million or more traded a day on average over 50 days.
facts.claim: Liquidity: a close of $10 or more and $20 million a day over 50 days.

facts.quote: A real correction first: the lowest close of the last 60 sessions is at least 15% under the highest high of the 60 sessions before that.
facts.claim: A real correction first: the lowest close of the last 60 sessions at least 15% under the prior 60 sessions' high.

facts.quote: A long base: at least 25 sessions (5 weeks) of closes within 10% of the bundle's middle.
facts.claim: A long base: at least 25 sessions of closes within 10% of the bundle's middle.

facts.quote: The last 30 closes span no more than 20% of price.
facts.claim: The last 30 closes span no more than 20% of price.

facts.quote: Fewer than 20 of the prior 40 closes are above the highest of the three averages.
facts.claim: Fewer than 20 of the prior 40 closes sit above the highest of the three averages.

facts.quote: The bundle is tight: the 8 EMA, 21 EMA and 50 SMA lie within 3% of price of each other on the day before the launch.
facts.claim: Tight: the bundle's three averages lie within 3% of price of each other the day before the launch.

facts.quote: The 200-day is close: within 10% of the bundle's middle on the day before the launch. Better: at or just under the bundle.
facts.claim: The 200-day is close, within 10% of the bundle's middle; better at or just under the bundle.

facts.quote: The launch bar closes above all four averages: the 8, 21, 50 and the 200. A close inside the bundle or under the 200-day is not the launch.
facts.claim: The launch bar closes above all four averages; a close inside the bundle or under the 200-day is not the launch.

facts.quote: The launch bar is a real push: up 2% or more on the day.
facts.claim: The launch bar is up 2% or more on the day.

facts.claim: The launch bar closes in the top 35% of its range, 0.65 or higher.

facts.quote: Volume of 2 times the 50-day average or more is the A+ version of the launch bar, not a rule.
facts.claim: Volume of 2 times the 50-day average is the A+ launch bar, not a rule.

facts.quote: Not a gap or news bar: the launch opens no more than 6% above the prior close and is not a one-off macro or news day. A bigger gap is a different setup (Kicker, earnings gap).
facts.claim: The launch opens no more than 6% above the prior close and is not a news bar; a bigger gap is another setup.

facts.claim: No new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report.

facts.claim: Launchpads come out of long bases and tend to trend along the 21-day.

walkthroughs.title: KBH, September 2004: the textbook pad
steps: KBH corrected 24.8% over four months in 2004. Then it spent two months going sideways around a flat 200-day.
Through that rest its averages pinch together, within 3% of each other. That tight bundle is the pad.
September 1 it launches: up 2.5%, closing near its high, over all four averages. Fill 35.26, stop under the low, 34.26.
Trade back through the launch day's low and it's wrong. Instead 3R came in seven sessions. The first sell is your call.

walkthroughs.title: BABA, January 2025: under the bundle, then the launch
steps: BABA fell 31.6%, then sat under its pinched averages. 26 of the last 40 closes were under the bundle, none above.
And the 200-day sits just 1% away. Weeks under a tight bundle with the 200 right there, that's the picture.
January 24, 2025: up 3.5%, closing at its high over all four. Fill 89.14, stop just under the low, 86.43.
Its averages lined up in order within 3 sessions. 3R came in three. That's a push worth selling some into.

walkthroughs.title: DDOG, October 2024: the drift, the trail and the time stop
steps: DDOG corrected 22.1% and pinched into a tight bundle. October 4, 2024, it launches up 4.4%, closing near the high.
Fill 122.69, stop 118.32, 3.6% away. Wider than I like, so fewer shares. Never pull the stop in to fit.
Then it drifts along its rising averages for four weeks. Over 1R inside 10 days, so the time stop stays quiet.
3R took 33 sessions. Pads come out of long bases and trend steadily, so you trail this one on the 20 EMA.

questions.q: What setup are you looking at here?
choices: A launchpad off a long rest
A flat base near the highs
A bull flag after a run
A V rally into the averages
questions.answer: A launchpad off a long rest
questions.why: That's a launchpad. KBH fell 24.8%, then sat for two months around a flat 200-day. Watch the averages through that rest. The three short ones pinch to within about 3% of each other, close to the 200. That pinch is the pad. I want weeks of it before I care about a launch. The next day KBH pushed up 2.5% and closed above all four lines. That was the launch.
questions.lesson_line: Hard fall, long rest, averages pinch. That's the pad. The launch comes after.

wrong.A flat base near the highs: A flat base sits near its highs, above the 50-day. This one fell hard and rested under its averages.
wrong.A bull flag after a run: A flag needs a sharp run up first. This stock fell first, then rested.
wrong.A V rally into the averages: A V rally rips straight back with no rest. This one sat for two months while its averages pinched.

questions.simple: It's a launchpad, a hard fall and then weeks of rest while the averages pinch together. The launch comes after that.

reasons: the long rest and the tight bundle are the unit's proposed card lines, with TraderLion's four steps as the outside view

questions.story: This stock fell hard. Then it sat for two months around a flat 200-day while its shorter averages squeezed together. The chart stops the day before the move.

deeper.counter: TraderLion lays out the same path in four steps: price trades under the averages in a base, reclaims them, the averages curl up under price, then price retests them and bounces.

questions.q: What happened before this rest?
choices: A deep correction, a real fall
A new high on big volume
A small dip, then a bounce
A steady climb over the 50-day
questions.answer: A deep correction, a real fall
questions.why: A real fall. RMD dropped 21.1% before it started resting. That matters because a pad is a stock repairing itself. The fall leaves the averages up above price. Then weeks of sideways action drag them down and pinch them together. No fall, nothing to repair, no pad. A dip inside an uptrend is a pullback, and we trade that with its own rules.
questions.lesson_line: No fall, no pad. The rest comes after the damage.

wrong.A small dip, then a bounce: A small dip in an uptrend is a pullback. We trade that one with its own rules.
wrong.A steady climb over the 50-day: Price riding on top of its averages is a pullback breakout, not a pad.
wrong.A new high on big volume: A pad comes after a fall. A stock making new highs is a different trade.

questions.simple: A real fall comes first. The pad is the stock resting and repairing after it got sold hard.

reasons: the 15% line is the unit's proposed card number and the near-miss note shows a second option under review

questions.story: Here's a stock the day before it launches. It spent about two months resting under its averages. Now look to the left of that rest.

questions.q: You bought this launch as it traded up through the averages. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Right, that's your stop. The low of the day is where this launch is wrong. If price trades back under it, the push failed and I want out. Go a few cents under it, not right on it, so one tick of noise doesn't take you out. Here that put the stop at 36.15. AIZ closed right at its high, 36.92, so even from the close that's only about 2.1% of risk. A close stop also means the same risk buys more shares.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. A few cents under the low of the day.
questions.simple: True. The day's low is where the launch failed, and a close stop lets the same risk buy more shares.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
the launch day's low as the stop goes with the close entry that D-003 still holds open
fixed-width stop rule, wording could change if D-003 flips

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The launch bar closes above all ___ averages, the 200-day among them.
questions.answer: four
questions.why: Four. The launch bar closes above the 8, 21 and 50 averages and the 200-day. The rulebook agrees: no longs below the 200-day, bar one rare exception.
questions.lesson_line: Above all four, or it is not the launch.
questions.simple: The launch bar must close above the three bundle averages and the 200-day, so that makes four lines.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and the settled card line

questions.q: You've sold part of a launchpad into strength. It's a steady mover. Which line do you trail the rest on?
choices: The 20 EMA
The 9 EMA
The 50-day
The 200-day
questions.answer: The 20 EMA
questions.why: The 20 EMA. Pads come out of long bases and tend to trend steady, riding along the 20. So that's the line I give the rest of the position. Sell it on a close below the 20, not on a dip under it during the day. The 9 EMA hugs price. On a steady mover it shakes you out of a good trend early. I save the 9 for the fast ones.
questions.lesson_line: Steady pad, 20 EMA trail. Sell the close below it.

wrong.The 50-day: Too far away for a trail. You'd give back a big chunk of the gain before it ever sells.
wrong.The 200-day: The 200-day decides whether we buy at all. It's not a trail.
wrong.The 9 EMA: The 9 is for a fast mover. On a steady pad it shakes you out too early.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA. A steady pad trends along it, so a close below it means the trend has broken.

deeper.trap: The sell signal is a close below the 20 EMA, not a dip under it during the day. Use the 9 EMA only for a fast mover.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52 trail)

questions.q: Two textbook pads launch the same day, one in a slow bank, one in a group leader. The bank's pad grades lower.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The pad is only the timing. The stock, the base and the market carry the edge. A leader in a strong group has buyers who want it, and a slow bank doesn't move like that. CMCSA printed a big-volume launch in a slow large cap and fell right back into its averages. Our grade is how clean we judge the setup, and the grade sets the size. So the bank gets less, or nothing.
questions.lesson_line: The pad is the shape. The stock is the trade.
questions.simple: True. A slow bank lacks the buyers a leader has, so the same pad earns a lower grade and a smaller size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D40) and the card's grade rule

questions.q: This launch bar clears all four averages but is still under the top of its base. It still counts as the launch.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Yes, it counts. A pad's event is clearing the averages, not breaking a base high. The stock spent weeks under those lines, so getting over all four is what ends the rest. The bar can still sit inside the base. Wait for the base high and you often pay a lot more for the same idea.
questions.lesson_line: The launch is clearing the averages, not the top of the base.
questions.simple: True. The pad is a rest under the averages, so clearing them is the launch, not a base high.

reasons: rests on the unit's card (c16, c33) alone

questions.q: Where's the 200-day sitting against that bundle?
choices: Right at it, or just under it
Far above it, like a ceiling
Far below it, way off
Anywhere, it doesn't matter
questions.answer: Right at it, or just under it
questions.why: Right at it. Here the 200-day sat just 0.8% from the bundle, so all four lines were in one tight band. That's what I want. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, so the launch has to clear it too. With the 200 sitting right in the bundle, one push clears all four lines at once. A 200-day far overhead is a ceiling you'd have to fight through after you buy.
questions.lesson_line: I want the 200-day right in the bundle. One push clears everything.

wrong.Far above it, like a ceiling: That's a ceiling over the launch. Price would have to fight through it after you buy.
wrong.Far below it, way off: Not on this chart. It sat 0.8% from the bundle. A 200-day far from the pinch grades lower. I want it right in there.
wrong.Anywhere, it doesn't matter: It matters a lot. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, so the launch has to clear it.

questions.simple: Right at the bundle. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, so you want one push to clear all four lines at once.

deeper.example: RDDT, in a July Sunday Scans note: 'The 200SMA remount was attractive out of this mini base here but it is still curling lower.' And: 'If we get a launchpad to form I will be increasingly more interested in it.'

reasons: the 10% line is the unit's card number
the RDDT note is the owner's published wording

questions.story: The day before a launch. The three short averages are pinched together into one tight bundle.

questions.q: How long is a launchpad base, at least?
choices: 25 sessions, about five weeks
5 sessions, about one week
10 sessions, about two weeks
100 sessions, about five months
questions.answer: 25 sessions, about five weeks
questions.why: At least 25 sessions, about five weeks, with closes within 10% of the bundle's middle. That is the floor for a launchpad base. A tight range of only a few days under the fast averages is a wedge pop, a different setup.
questions.lesson_line: Five weeks or more under the bundle. Days are a wedge pop, not a pad.

wrong.5 sessions, about one week: A tight range of a few days under the fast averages is a wedge pop, not a launchpad.
wrong.10 sessions, about two weeks: Two weeks is a pause, not a pad. The rule is 25 sessions.
wrong.100 sessions, about five months: That asks for far more than the rule. The floor is 25 sessions.

questions.simple: A launchpad base lasts at least 25 sessions, about five weeks, so a few days under the averages is too short.

reasons: the 25-session floor is the unit's card number

questions.q: A stock creeps over its averages on a quiet, flat day. That's not the push I want from a launch bar.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The launch is the day buyers take the stock from under its averages to over them in one session. I want to see that in the bar: a real move up, closing near the top of its range. A quiet creep proves nothing and can slip right back inside the next day. It doesn't need to be huge. AIZ's launch was only up 2.0%, but it closed right at the high.
questions.lesson_line: I want a real push off the pad, not a drift.
questions.simple: True. A real push over the averages in one day shows buyers stepping in, and a quiet drift proves little.

deeper.counter: A bigger push is no guarantee. The four failures had launch bars of +4.6% to +5.6% on 1.8x to 2.6x volume, closing in the top third. Nothing on the bar separated them from the ten winners. The stock, the base and the market carry the edge.

reasons: the 2% floor is the unit's card number

questions.q: Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
Under the base low, at full size
Right at your buy price
Wherever your usual size fits
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the low of the day. That's where this launch is wrong. If it trades back under the day's low, the push failed. On CMC that put the stop at 16.01, about 4.1% under the 16.69 buy. That's wider than the 1% to 3% I like, but inside the 5% we take, so you buy fewer shares. A stop under the base low or the averages is allowed, but it sits further down still. Put full size on a stop that far away and a normal loss turns into a big one. A stop at your buy is breakeven, and that comes later.
questions.lesson_line: The low of the day is your stop. Size from it, never the other way round.

wrong.Right at your buy price: That's breakeven. You move the stop up there later, between 2R and 5R or at your first sell.
wrong.Under the base low, at full size: The base low can be a fair stop, but it sits far under your buy. Full size there risks way more than you planned.
wrong.Wherever your usual size fits: That's backwards. The chart sets the stop, and the stop sets the size.

questions.simple: A few cents under the day's low. That's where the launch failed, and your size comes from that stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13 stop habit, D41, A4)

questions.story: Launch day. You bought as price traded up through the averages.

questions.q: Your launchpad trade is up 5R and the company reports tomorrow. You can hold it through the report.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True, and 5R is the line. A report can gap a stock way past your stop overnight. Your stop can't catch a gap. Being up 5R is the cushion. If the report goes wrong, the gap eats into profit, not into your account. Under 5R, I'm out before the report. And no new buys in the 3 days before one.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R, you can hold through earnings. Under that, you're out before the report.
questions.simple: True. A report can gap the stock past your stop, and being up 5R is the cushion that can take that hit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The bundle's three averages lie within ___% of price of each other on the day before the launch.
questions.why: 3%. Tight means the bundle's three averages lie within 3% of price of each other on the day before the launch. If the averages are not tight, it is not a launchpad.
questions.lesson_line: Tight is a number here: three percent of price across the three lines.
questions.simple: The three bundle averages must sit within 3% of price of each other, or the pad is not tight enough.

deeper.trap: The 3% is measured against price, not against one average. Take the highest of the three averages minus the lowest, divide by price, on the day before the launch.

reasons: the 3% line is the unit's card number

questions.q: What are you looking at?
choices: A breakout, not a launchpad
A launchpad, it cleared all four
The fastest kind of launchpad
A wedge pop off a tight range
questions.answer: A breakout, not a launchpad
questions.why: A breakout, not a launchpad. The stock never rested. A pad is weeks of sideways action under the averages while they pinch together. This went straight up from 25% below them. The bar that cleared all four can look exactly like a launch. That's the trap. So before I look at the bar, I count the weeks of rest underneath it. No rest, no pad.
questions.lesson_line: A V straight into the averages is a breakout wearing a pad's name.

wrong.The fastest kind of launchpad: Speed doesn't help here. A pad is a slow rest under pinched averages.
wrong.A wedge pop off a tight range: A wedge pop needs a few tight days under the fast averages. This went straight up from far below.
wrong.A launchpad, it cleared all four: Clearing all four is only the launch bar. The pad is the weeks of rest before it, and there weren't any.

questions.story: A stock fell 25% below its averages. Then it ripped straight back up into them and closed above all four within a week.
questions.simple: A breakout. It never rested under the averages, so there was no pad to launch from.

deeper.trap: Do not judge by the launch bar alone. A V rally can close above all four averages with a strong green bar and look just like a launch. What it lacks is the weeks of tight rest underneath. Count the sessions under the bundle before you call it a pad.

reasons: rests on the unit's card lines (c23, c03)
question stem reworded to remove a tell

questions.q: A clean pad sets up in a stock that trades 3,000,000 shares a day. What's the most shares you'd ever own?
choices: 30,000 shares
300,000 shares
3,000 shares
150,000 shares
questions.answer: 30,000 shares
questions.why: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. It's about getting out. Hold a big slice of a day's volume and you can't sell fast without pushing the price down on yourself. That's a ceiling, not a target. Your stop and your risk still set the actual size.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, max. I want to be able to get out.

wrong.300,000 shares: That's ten times the ceiling. You'd be a big part of every day's trading.
wrong.3,000 shares: That's a tenth of the ceiling. You can own it, but it's not the max.
wrong.150,000 shares: That's five times over the cap.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares. Never more than 1% of daily volume, so you can get out without pushing the price down on yourself.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)
fixed before: a wrong note was reworded in the cold check

questions.q: A wide, loose stock with huge daily swings sets up a pad. That big range makes it a better launchpad buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. That's a trap. When a stock swings that much on an ordinary day, it crosses its averages all the time. So pinched lines and a bar over them don't tell you much. The stop is a problem too. The low of the day can be a long way under your buy, and that cuts your size. I want a tight, orderly stock for a pad.
questions.lesson_line: Wide and loose is a trap. I want a tight, orderly stock for a pad.
questions.simple: False. A wide, loose stock crosses its averages on normal days, so a pad in it proves little.

reasons: the card's grade rule (c31)

deeper.counter: Ross Haber says the same in his launchpad guide: wide, loose stocks with huge average daily ranges can form something that looks like a launchpad, but it's often a trap.

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, Orange is A+ setups only
Yes, a clean launch beats the market
Yes, at half the usual size
No, Orange means all cash
questions.answer: No, Orange is A+ setups only
questions.why: No. Orange means the market is under pressure, and breakouts fail more when the market isn't backing them. So in Orange I only want my very best ideas, the A+ ones. This one's a B. It can wait for a better market. Orange isn't all cash, though. The A+ setups still get bought. Green is when we press, and Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange is A+ only. Everything else waits for a better market.

wrong.Yes, a clean launch beats the market: The launch is clean, but the market isn't backing breakouts. In Orange a B waits.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Size isn't the fix. In Orange it's about the grade, and a B sits out.
wrong.No, Orange means all cash: That's Red, mostly cash. Orange still takes the A+ setups.

questions.story: The app's market filter turned Orange this week, one step from Red. The market's under pressure. A launchpad fires today, and on your grading it's a B, a good setup but not your best.
questions.simple: No. In Orange breakouts fail more, so we only take A+ setups, and this one is a B.

deeper.trap: Orange is not Red. In Red the long version is off and the book is mostly cash and shorts. In Orange the A+ launchpads still trade, so the reading narrows the grade you accept, not whether you trade at all.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A10 market reading)

questions.q: We scanned 2,417 launchpads. Most of them ran to 5R before they hit the stop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False, not even close. Only 14.6% of the 2,417 reached 5R, and just 26.6% reached 3R. Most launches don't go anywhere. That's normal, and it's why the stop under the low of the day matters so much. Each miss costs you 1R. The few that run pay for all of them. Know that going in, and a string of small losers won't shake you.
questions.lesson_line: Most pads don't run. Small losses on the misses, big wins on the few that do.
questions.simple: False. Only a small share reached 5R, so we keep each loss small and let the few runners pay for the rest.

deeper.counter: All ten worked examples reached 5R before the fixed stop. The scan of 2,417 launches says only 14.6% did.

questions.why: No. The last 30 closes must span no more than 20% of price, and 24% is more. That is a loose base, not a pad. A tight bundle cannot fix it, because the span is its own test and both have to pass.
questions.lesson_line: A pad is a flat rest. A 24% swing is not flat.

wrong.Yes; wide bases are stronger: The rule caps the span at 20% of price. A base this wide is not a flat rest.
wrong.Yes, if the bundle is tight: A tight bundle is a separate test from the span. Both have to pass.
wrong.No; the span rule is 10% of price: That mixes two tests. 10% is the band around the bundle's middle for the base length. The span rule is 20% of price.

questions.simple: No, because the last 30 closes may span only 20% of price, and these span 24%.

reasons: one cited fact only for the key
the 20% span line is a proposed card number

questions.q: As long as you're watching the screen, a stop kept in your head works fine on a launchpad.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Every position gets a real stop order with the broker. A stop in your head turns into a debate the second price hits it. You tell yourself to see if it holds, and a small loss turns into a big one. And you can't watch every tick. An order sells for you at the level you chose, whether you're watching or not.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False. A stop in your head gets argued with when price hits it, and an order with the broker just sells.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: What was that?
choices: A fake-out, not a failure
A failure, sell the first close
A new launch, add to it
A break, take it off the list
questions.answer: A fake-out, not a failure
questions.why: A fake-out. Quick break, quick reclaim. That's noise, not a failure. Once you're in, the stop is your exit, and price never got there. Sell that close under the averages and you'd have been shaken out of a trade that was fine. And the reclaim isn't a new buy or a reason to add. Same trade, same position.
questions.lesson_line: A one-day dip under the averages is noise. The stop makes the call.

wrong.A failure, sell the first close: Once you're in, the stop is the exit, and it never traded.
wrong.A new launch, add to it: Same trade, not a new buy. We buy full size at one price, and a reclaim is no reason to add.
wrong.A break, take it off the list: Off the list is for before you buy. Now the stop decides.

questions.story: Two days after the launch, the stock closes back under the averages. It's still above your stop. The next day it closes back over them.
questions.simple: A fake-out. Price never hit your stop, and the stop is your only exit.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (a quick break and reclaim is a fake-out)

questions.q: A really clean pad sets up in an $8 stock that trades about $6 million a day. Do you take it?
choices: No, under $10 and $20 million a day
Yes, a clean pad is a clean pad
Yes, but with a small size
No, the 1% volume cap blocks it
questions.answer: No, under $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: No. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. This one's $8 and does $6 million, so it fails both. Thin stocks are hard to get out of at a fair price. Your stop can slip, and you can't hold much. A clean chart doesn't change any of that. I don't even watch names like this.
questions.lesson_line: A clean pad in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes, a clean pad is a clean pad: Liquidity comes before the chart. We don't even watch thin stocks.
wrong.Yes, but with a small size: Small size doesn't make a thin stock liquid.
wrong.No, the 1% volume cap blocks it: Right call, wrong rule. The 1% cap sizes a stock that already passed. This one fails the $10 and $20 million screen first.

questions.simple: No. It's under $10 and under $20 million a day, too thin to get in and out of cleanly.

deeper.counter: The $10 and $20 million rule screens the stock. The 1% of daily volume rule caps the size inside a stock that passed. They are two separate rules, and passing one never excuses the other.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23 liquidity screen)

questions.q: Launchpad or wedge pop?
choices: A wedge pop, days not weeks
A launchpad, it cleared the averages
Neither, the fall was too deep
A flat base, the range is tight
questions.answer: A wedge pop, days not weeks
questions.why: A wedge pop. Four days is a pause, not a pad. A launchpad rests for weeks, long enough for the averages to pinch together near the 200-day. A wedge pop is a few tight days under the fast averages after a drop, and the pop takes back those two lines. Different setup, different plan. Count the sessions before you name it.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions. A pad is weeks, a wedge pop is days.

wrong.A launchpad, it cleared the averages: Clearing two fast lines after four days is a wedge pop. A pad needs weeks under all of them.
wrong.Neither, the fall was too deep: A deep fall is fine for both. How long it rested tells them apart.
wrong.A flat base, the range is tight: A flat base sits above the 50-day near its highs. This one fell 30% first.

questions.story: After a 30% fall the stock holds a tight four-day range under its two fast averages. Then it pops over them.
questions.simple: A wedge pop. Four days is too short for a pad, which needs weeks under pinched averages.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines (wedge pop, 25-session base)

questions.q: Is this a launchpad?
choices: No, the dip was too shallow
Yes, the averages pinched
Yes, it's above the 200-day
No, a strong day isn't a launch
questions.answer: No, the dip was too shallow
questions.why: No. A pad comes out of real damage, a deep fall and a long repair. This was an 11.2% dip with the 200-day still rising underneath. That's a pullback in an uptrend, and we trade it as a moving average pullback, with its own entry and stop. The pads that work come after real falls. KBH fell 24.8% and BABA 31.6% before theirs. Pinched averages alone don't make it a pad.
questions.lesson_line: A dip in an uptrend is a pullback. A pad comes after real damage.

wrong.Yes, the averages pinched: Averages pinch in pullbacks too. A pad needs the real fall first.
wrong.Yes, it's above the 200-day: Being over the 200-day is the starting point for any long. It doesn't make a pullback a pad.
wrong.No, a strong day isn't a launch: A strong day over the averages is exactly what a launch looks like. The problem is the shallow dip.

questions.story: The stock dipped 11.2% from its high, staying over a rising 200-day. The averages pinch, then a strong day closes above them.
questions.simple: No. A shallow dip in an uptrend is a pullback, not the real fall a pad comes out of.

deeper.example: The tell is the order of events. A pad is a rest after a fall. A pullback is a dip inside a rising trend. This one fell 11.2% over a rising 200-day, so it was a moving-average pullback, not a pad, even with the averages pinched.

reasons: the 15% correction line is a proposed card number

questions.q: Is this a launchpad?
choices: No, the averages never pinched
Yes, 2.78x volume makes it A+
Yes, it cleared the averages
No, a 4.8% bar is too big
questions.answer: No, the averages never pinched
questions.why: Not a pad. The averages never pinched. They were 5.77% of price apart the day before. On pads that worked they were tight: 2.91% on KBH, 1.86% on BABA. A big bar on big volume through loose averages is just a rally bar. Volume raises the grade of a real launch. It can't create the pad. And it was still under a falling 200-day, where we don't buy stocks anyway.
questions.lesson_line: No pinch, no pad. A big bar through loose averages is just a big bar.

wrong.Yes, 2.78x volume makes it A+: Volume raises the grade of a real launch. Without the pinch there's no pad to grade.
wrong.Yes, it cleared the averages: It cleared loose averages and stayed under a falling 200-day. That's a rally bar.
wrong.No, a 4.8% bar is too big: A big bar is fine. Loose averages are the problem.

questions.story: The day before, the three short averages sit 5.77% of price apart. Then a bar up 4.8% on 2.78x volume pushes through them, still under a falling 200-day.
questions.simple: No. The averages were loose, not pinched, so a big bar through them is just a rally.

deeper.trap: A big bar on big volume draws the eye. The real test comes the day before: have the averages pinched together? Here they were 5.77% of price apart. Skip that check and a rally bar gets called a launch.

reasons: the 3% bundle width is a proposed card number

questions.q: Price has been riding on top of the three averages, and they're tight. That makes this bar a launchpad.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Look where price sat. On top of tight averages in an uptrend is a pullback breakout, not a pad. In a pad, price rests under the averages for weeks while they pinch, and the launch clears them. Here the averages are support that price has been riding. That's a different trade with its own entry and stop. Tight lines alone don't make it a pad.
questions.lesson_line: Price on top of tight averages is a pullback. A pad has price under them.
questions.simple: False. In a pad price rests under the averages, and riding on top of them is a pullback breakout.

deeper.counter: Tight averages can still sit under price. That is price riding on top of the bundle in an uptrend, a pullback breakout. A launchpad is the other way round: its closes sit under the averages first.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (price riding on top of the bundle is a pullback breakout)

questions.q: What's your read on this one?
choices: Right bar, wrong kind of stock
The volume lied, skip 2x bars
The stop was too tight, widen it
The 16% fall was too shallow
questions.answer: Right bar, wrong kind of stock
questions.why: Right bar, wrong stock. Every number on the setup passed: a real fall, a tight pinch, a real push, heavy volume. But CMCSA is a slow large cap, and those don't get the buyers a leader gets. The bar is only the timing. The stock, the base and the market carry the edge. So read the stock first. I want a leader or a name in a strong group. The good news: the stop did its job, 1R and out.
questions.lesson_line: The bar is the timing. The stock, the base and the market are the edge.

wrong.The volume lied, skip 2x bars: Heavy volume still raises the grade. It just can't fix a slow stock.
wrong.The stop was too tight, widen it: The stop under the launch day's low did its job, 1R and out. Stops never get widened.
wrong.The 16% fall was too shallow: The fall was real. A deeper one wouldn't have saved a slow large cap.

questions.story: A 16% fall, averages pinched to 0.83%, then a launch up 4.9% on 2.17x volume in a slow large cap. One flat day, then two red days back into the averages took the stop.
questions.simple: The launch bar looked fine, but a slow large cap lacks the buyers a leader has. The stop kept it to 1R.

deeper.trap: The bar cannot tell you the stock. The four failures had launch bars of +4.6% to +5.6% on 1.8x to 2.6x volume, closing in the top third. A strong bar did not keep a slow large cap from failing. So read the stock first: a leader or a stock in a strong group, not a slow bank.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines (stock quality, grade down for slow names)

questions.q: How many R are you up?
questions.why: 5R. Your gain is 102.69 minus 89.14. Your 1R is 89.14 minus 86.43. Divide the gain by 1R and you get 5. Counting in R shows how the trade's doing against what you risked, so different stops compare fairly. 5R is where I start thinking about a first sell. About 5 to 10R is often a good spot. The sell itself is still your call.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. Around 5R I start thinking about selling.
questions.simple: 5R, the gain is five times what you risked from buy to stop. About 5 to 10R is often a good place to sell.

deeper.trap: R is counted from the fill, not from the stop. Counting from the stop counts the risk itself as gain, so it reads one R too high. A dollar gain misleads too: it means nothing until you divide it by the risk per share. Five R is a yardstick, not an automatic sale.

wrong.0.2R: That divides the gain by the price, not by your risk.
wrong.2.7R: That's your risk per share, not the R count.
wrong.4.0R: You took one R off the gain before dividing.

questions.q: Launchpad or flat base?
choices: A flat base, it broke its own high
A launchpad, the averages are close
Both, it's the same thing
A VCP, it held a rising 50-day
questions.answer: A flat base, it broke its own high
questions.why: A flat base. Look where the closes sat: over a rising 50-day, in a box near the highs. That's a flat base, and you buy it as it trades through the top of the box. A pad is the opposite. It sits under its averages for weeks after a fall, and the launch clears them. The name matters because the trigger and the stop are different.
questions.lesson_line: Check where the closes sat. Over the 50-day in a box is a flat base.

wrong.A launchpad, the averages are close: Close isn't under. A pad spends weeks under its averages. This one never did.
wrong.Both, it's the same thing: Different setups, different triggers. A pad clears its averages, a flat base breaks its own high.
wrong.A VCP, it held a rising 50-day: A VCP shows pullbacks that get smaller and smaller. This is one flat box.

questions.story: For nine weeks every close held over a rising 50-day, inside a box near the highs. Today it trades through the top of the box.
questions.simple: A flat base. It held over its 50-day near the highs and broke through the top of its box.

deeper.counter: Look where the closes sat. A flat base holds above the 50-day and breaks out over its own highest high. A pad rests under the bundle, and its launch is the close above it.

reasons: rests on a proposed card lookalike line
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: If the first 30 minutes of a gap-down day take the loss past 2R, you get out.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The first 30-minute low is the new stop; out if that is past 2R.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule has a ceiling. Two R, and you are out.

questions.q: Does the time stop kick in?
choices: No, it's over 1R, so it stays
Yes, ten days and no 3R
Yes, sell half of it
No, any gain at all keeps it
questions.answer: No, it's over 1R, so it stays
questions.why: No. The time stop is for trades that aren't doing anything: still under 1R after 10 trading days, you sell and free the money. This one's over 1R, so it's working, just slowly. The test is 1R, not 3R. Leave it alone. DDOG took 33 sessions to reach 3R and ended up running to 10.8R.
questions.lesson_line: The time stop asks for 1R, not 3R. A slow pad that's working gets left alone.

wrong.Yes, ten days and no 3R: The bar is 1R, not 3R. Over 1R in ten days means it's working.
wrong.Yes, sell half of it: There's no half sale here. Under 1R it goes, over 1R it stays.
wrong.No, any gain at all keeps it: It's 1R, not any profit. A trade up a little but under 1R after 10 days gets sold.

questions.story: You bought the launch at 122.69 with the stop at 118.32. For four weeks it hangs around its short averages. By day ten it's over 1R but nowhere near 3R.
questions.simple: No, it's over 1R by day ten, so it's working. The time stop only frees money from trades that aren't.

deeper.example: DDOG, launch 2024-10-04: bought 122.69, stop 118.32. It dangled near its short averages for four weeks. 3R took 33 sessions, yet it was over 1R inside 10 days. It ran to 10.8R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33 time stop)

questions.q: What do you do with the rest?
choices: Sell it on this close under the 20
Hold, the stop's at breakeven
Hold until it closes under the 50
Sell after a second close under it
questions.answer: Sell it on this close under the 20
questions.why: Sell it. The rest of a steady mover rides the 20 EMA, and a close under it gets you out. A pad that trended along the 20 just lost it. The trend that carried you has broken, so you take the gain while it's still there. One close is the signal. Breakeven is only your floor. The trail is how you get out with the money.
questions.lesson_line: Part's banked, the rest is on the trail. The close under the line is the exit.

wrong.Hold, the stop's at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for the rest.
wrong.Hold until it closes under the 50: A steady mover trails the 20 EMA. Waiting for the 50 gives back a lot.
wrong.Sell after a second close under it: One close under the 20 is the signal.

questions.story: You've sold part into strength. Today the rest, a steady mover, closes under the 20 EMA for the first time since the launch.
questions.simple: Sell it. A close under the 20 EMA means the trend that carried the trade has broken.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52 trail)

questions.q: Do you buy it again?
choices: Yes, as a new trade with a new stop
No, each pad gets one try
Yes, with a wider stop this time
No, wait a week to cool off
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade with a new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a brand new trade. The stop-out only said that launch failed. Thursday's bar is a new launch, so it gets its own plan: a new stop a few cents under that day's low, sized from scratch. Taking a second shot is normal. We cap it at 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. That keeps one stubborn name from bleeding the account.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. The next launch is a new trade.

wrong.No, each pad gets one try: You get up to 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: The new trade gets its own honest stop under the new low of the day. Wider just means fewer shares.
wrong.No, wait a week to cool off: There's no waiting period. What matters is a new trigger.

questions.story: You got stopped out of a launchpad on Tuesday. Thursday it pushes back up through all four averages, up 3% on the day, on volume.
questions.simple: Yes, if it triggers again. The stop-out ended that launch, and a new launch is a fresh trade with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is the stop. The new trade needs its own honest stop, a few cents under the new launch day's low. Widening it only means fewer shares. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: On daily bars the launch bar alone is the edge; the base and the stock are secondary.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The launch bar looks the same on winners and losers. The stock, the base and the market are the edge, and the launch bar only times the entry. In the dossier's failures the launch bars matched the winners' bars.
questions.lesson_line: The bar times the trade. The stock, the base and the market decide it.
questions.simple: False, because the launch bar looks the same on winners and losers, so the stock, base and market carry the edge.

deeper.counter: A 2x launch bar was not a protection. TEAM closed up 4.1% on 2.13x volume and was stopped the next session. The failures had launch bars of +4.6% to +5.6% on 1.8x to 2.6x volume, just like the winners.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines (the bar is not the edge)

questions.q: Is this the launch?
choices: No; the day is under the 2% push
Yes; the close and volume carry it
Yes; above all four is enough
No; volume must reach 2x to count
questions.answer: No; the day is under the 2% push
questions.why: No. The launch bar is a real push, up 2% or more on the day. This bar was up 1.5%. Closing above all four averages is one test and the push is another, and the push failed. A strong close and 1.8x volume cannot replace the push.
questions.lesson_line: Every launch test has to pass. A quiet day above the averages is a wait.

wrong.Yes; the close and volume carry it: The close and the volume are separate tests. They do not make a 1.5% day a push.
wrong.Yes; above all four is enough: Above all four is one test. Up 2% or more is another, and it failed.
wrong.No; volume must reach 2x to count: 2x volume is the A+ version, not a rule. This bar fails on the 2% push, not on volume.

questions.story: A pad prints a +1.5% day that closes at 0.9 of its range on 1.8x volume, above all four averages.
questions.simple: No, because a launch must be up 2% or more on the day, and this bar was up only 1.5%.

reasons: the 2% push is a proposed card number

questions.q: Same pads otherwise. The 200-day is 9% under the bundle's middle on one, 12% under on the other. Which passes the 200-day test?
choices: The 9% pad only; within 10%
The 12% pad only; more room
Both; the line is within 15%
Neither; it must sit on the bundle
questions.answer: The 9% pad only; within 10%
questions.why: The 9% pad only. The 200-day must be within 10% of the bundle's middle on the day before the launch. 9% passes. 12% is outside the line, so that 200-day is too far away. Better is at or just under the bundle, but that is a grade, not the gate.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day must sit within 10% of the bundle. Nine percent passes. Twelve does not.

wrong.The 12% pad only; more room: Room is not the point. 12% is outside the 10% line, so that 200-day is too far from the bundle.
wrong.Neither; it must sit on the bundle: The line is within 10%, not on the bundle. At or just under the bundle is the better grade, not the gate.
wrong.Both; the line is within 15%: The line is within 10%, not 15%. The 12% pad is outside it, so that 200-day is too far from the bundle.

questions.simple: The pad with the 200-day 9% away passes, because the line is within 10%. The 12% pad does not.

deeper.trap: Both pads look close, so it is easy to pass both. The line is a clean 10%: 9% is in and 12% is out. The card also calls at or just under the bundle better, but that is a grade, not the gate.

questions.q: Write your plan: entry, stop, first sell.
choices: Through the trigger, day's low, day 3
Limit under price, day's low, day 1
Next open, 200-day stop, day 3
At the close, base-low stop, day 1

questions.why: Buy it as it trades through the trigger, during the day, with a market order. Stop a few cents under the low of the day. On CME that put the stop at 38.61. From the 39.60 close, that's about 2.5%, right where I like it. The first sell is a judgment. I very rarely sell before day 3, and the best ones often come into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Write all three down before you buy. Then there's nothing to debate when the stock's moving fast.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell. Know them before you buy.

wrong.Limit under price, day's low, day 1: Entries are market orders through the trigger. And we very rarely sell on day 1.
wrong.Next open, 200-day stop, day 3: The buy is through the trigger that day, not the next open. The stop goes under the day's low.
wrong.At the close, base-low stop, day 1: We buy through the trigger, never at the close. The base low is too far, and day 1 is too early.

questions.story: Weeks of closes under the averages after a big fall. Today it's up 3.6% and pushing through all four.
questions.simple: Buy through the trigger, stop under the day's low, no sell before day 3. Plan it first so nothing gets decided under pressure.

deeper.trap: The trap is the stop. A stop under the averages or the base is allowed, but it sits far from the buy. Size from it and you get a tiny position. Pull it in to fit more shares and you've made the classic mistake. The low of the day is the stop.

questions.q: Here's the chart the day before a possible launch. Is this a pad you'd watch, or a pass?

Pass, it rode on top of the averages
Pass, the 200-day is too far away
Watch it, it's a flat base

wrong.Pass, the 200-day is too far away: 4.9% from the bundle is close enough.
wrong.Watch it, it's a flat base: A flat base holds over the 50-day. These closes sat under the averages.

questions.q: Is this the launch? Take it or pass.

Take it, it cleared the averages
Take it, 1.25x volume is enough
Pass, volume is under 2x

questions.simple: True. Haber waits past 3%, while we prefer 1% to 3% and accept up to 5%.

deeper.trap: Haber's 3% and ours are not the same line. His is a go or no-go on the entry: over 3% away, wait or pass. Ours is a range: 1% to 3% preferred, 3.5% good, up to 5% acceptable. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. Neither pulls the stop in to fit.

questions.q: What does B- do to your size?
questions.story: You grade this launchpad B-. Our grade is how clean we judge a setup, and it sets the size. The app's market filter reads Green, which allows full risk per grade.
choices: Smaller, B- gets the least risk
Normal, Green means full size
Bigger, the stop is close
Skip it, we never buy a B-
questions.answer: Smaller, B- gets the least risk

wrong.Normal, Green means full size: Green means full risk for each grade. A B- still gets sized down.
wrong.Bigger, the stop is close: A close stop gives more shares for the same risk. But a B- starts with less risk.
wrong.Skip it, we never buy a B-: We do buy a B-, just smaller. Orange is when we stick to A+.

questions.why: Smaller. The grade sets the size. A+ gets sized up, A and B are normal, and B- or lower gets sized down. In risk terms that's 0.25% to 0.5% on a B- against 0.5% to 1% on an A or B. A weaker setup works less often, so you want less riding on it. Green lets you take full risk for each grade. It doesn't turn a B- into an A.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the size. A+ up, A and B normal, B- down.
questions.simple: Smaller. The grade sets the size, and a B- is a weaker setup, so it gets the least risk.

deeper.trap: Green is not a bigger size for everything. The reading says how much the account may trade, and the grade says how much each setup gets. Grading stays our judgment, with no fixed checklist.

questions.q: What do you do with it?
questions.story: The app's market filter reads Red: mostly cash and shorts. A textbook pad launches in a real leader.
choices: Track it, wait for the market to turn
Buy it at half the usual size
Buy it, the pad is clean
Drop it from the list for good
questions.answer: Track it, wait for the market to turn

wrong.Buy it at half the usual size: Red is mostly cash. Half size is still fighting the market.
wrong.Drop it from the list for good: A leader basing in a weak market is the one to watch. Keep it.
wrong.Buy it, the pad is clean: The pad's clean, but the market isn't backing anything.

questions.why: Track it. Red means the market's dragging most stocks down with it, and we're mostly in cash. Even a great pad fights the whole market there. But don't throw it away. A leader that keeps basing while the market's weak is exactly what I want to own when it turns. Pads work best when leaders are basing as the reading turns Green. Keep it on your list and be ready.
questions.lesson_line: In Red the pad waits. Track the leader until the market turns.
questions.simple: Track it. Red keeps us mostly in cash, but a leader basing now is the one to buy when the market turns.
